Mr. President, distinguished members of the Executive Board, distinguished member states, colleagues, it's a pleasure to join you today in this important segment on UNOPS, following yesterday's very fruitful discussion with UNDP on the UN Haiti process. Since we last met, our world has continued its descent into crisis. Armed conflicts, the climate crisis, and economic instability have continued to deepen communities' needs around the world. 25% of the world's population currently live in conflict-affected settings. While poverty, inequality and anger are spreading. This comes as official development assistance has fallen sharply to historical low levels, dropping by nearly 23% compared to 2024. So the limits of the multilateral system are being tested. Against this background, it is more critical and timely than ever for the United Nations to continue providing practical solutions that improve people's lives, in particularly those most in need. As such, UNOPS continues to scale up and speed up project implementation with tangible results that bring an impact for the communities we serve. In today's session, I will highlight how UNOPS has responded to ongoing global challenges. I'd like to start by an element of enabling. One of the key functions that EUNOPS plays is not only delivering projects on infrastructure procurement project management, but also through our mandate enabling others to deliver. And I would like to provide a few examples starting with the current conflict raging across the Middle East region. To mitigate the humanitarian consequences of the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, The Secretary-General in March created a task force that I'm honored to lead with other UN agencies to facilitate the safe passage of fertilizers and related raw materials for humanitarian purposes. The case is very clear: one-third of the fertilizers in the world goes through the Strait of Hormuz, and the disruption of the fertilizers in the Strait of Hormuz is causing a global disruption of fertilizers. So it's no longer a regional crisis, it became a global crisis with impacts across all continents. We also noticed from— namely from FAO and WFP projections— that there is always a time lag between the increase of the prices on fertilizers and the impact on food. And unfortunately, as you used to say, it's written on the wall. If the current situation continues, very likely we'll get 45 million people being forced into acute food insecurity with massive impacts on poverty and inequality. That's why the Secretary-General launched this initiative to find a way not to compromise or undermine the freedom of navigation, but while we fight for freedom of navigation, at the same time finding a time-bound, exceptional, limited solution to allow fertilizers and related raw materials to transit, namely ammonia, urea, and sulfur. We are ready. From UN, and from UNOPS, we have developed the mechanism and we are ready in 7 days to put the mechanism functioning if the political will allows us. We see and we witness an increasing support for this mechanism by member states. Every day there is new member states issuing statements supporting the mechanism and I continue engaging, as you know, with the parties in the conflict and with the parties in the region to find a solution that would allow the mechanism to function. This is just one example, Mr. President and distinguished Member States, of UNOPS' role enabling. It draws on the same experience in Yemen with the UNV mechanism, the United Nations Verification and Inspection Mechanism for Yemen, but also the UN 2720 mechanism for Gaza. In both cases, what we are basically doing is confidence building, the same as we are trying to do in the Strait of Hormuz, is designing a mechanism to ensure accountability, transparency, and through that to build trust and confidence, and through that to allow humanitarian and also commercial flows to flow. Giving you one example, some data,— it's always important to bring data to these conversations. In Gaza Strip, with this mechanism, the 2720 mechanism that UNOPS is managing to help expedite and facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid, over 445,000 metric tonnes of aid have been delivered and tracked through the mechanism since its inception in April 2024, including 3,380 metric tonnes since the October 25 ceasefire. But some relevant data can also be shared from the UNV mechanism in Djibouti and Yemen. As you know, all transit of vessels going from Djibouti to Yemen, sailing to the Yemen ports of Hodeida Raziza and Salif are monitored, verified, and inspected by UNOPS in this initiative on behalf of, of concerned member states and OCHA. And the numbers are quite eloquent. Since it became operational in May 2016, UNVIM has successfully facilitated sailing for over 3,200 commercial vessels transporting over 73 million metric tons of essential goods. And we report the data to the Security Council. So this is, again, a confidence-building mechanism that allows us to monitor, to verify, and to inspect, and through that, to report to member states about the full implementation of the regulation. So I wanted to start this conversation precisely about this topic of enabling. Not very often it's the topic that I bring in these sessions. I tend to bring the topics about infrastructure, procurement, project management, and the concrete projects that we put on the place. But in this case, I really wanted to stress and emphasize how much we do to enable other UN agencies to operate, how much we do to enable Member States to operate, how much we do to enable commercial activities to operate. Let me now focus on the Annual Report 2025. Enabling our partners to deliver across humanitarian, peacebuilding, and development contexts is at the core of what we do. Our focus remains on implementation, on offering practical solutions. Our 2025 Annual Report, published this, this week, with copies in front of you, Highlights the scale and impact of this work. Last year, UNOPS worked in over 130 countries and territories, delivering over 1,100 projects worth approximately $2.7 billion. We created 26 million days of paid work for local communities, including 10 million days for women. Two-thirds of all our work was in compli— complex and fragile situations, where it's really hard to deliver. Allow me to share some examples. In Ukraine, our teams continue to support much-needed response and recovery efforts as communities face ongoing attacks and severe disruptions to basic services. Recently, we built a new anti-radiation shelter for a school in the southern Mikolaiv region. As a result, nearly 250 students and over 3,000 residents now have a safe underground space. For the first time in over 4 years, children will be able to attend their school in person, allowing them to reconnect with their childhood, learn, and thrive. In Gaza, in addition to supporting humanitarian deliveries through the implementation of the 2720 mechanism that I just mentioned. UNOPS also helps bring fuel in support to UN and humanitarian organizations, including hospitals, desalination plants, shelters, and immediate emergency needs. As you know, in Gaza, fuel is the only source of energy available. That's why this operation of procuring, distributing fuel is fundamental to the livelihood in Gaza. But let me stress the fact— and I will come to this later— that it is fundamental to provide early recovery support in Gaza. We can't wait for the reconstruction to do whatever we can to provide early recovery. UNOPS and UN Mine Action Service are supporting critical humanitarian aid efforts through mitigating the dangers of landmines and unexploded ordnance. And we stand ready to support the transition from humanitarian action to early recovery and eventual reconstruction, as I just mentioned. Just to give you some examples, because very often Member States ask me, 'What would early recovery look like? Are you ready to provide early recovery?' And we have indeed a concrete list of projects ready to implement including the provision of prefabs to provide proper sheltering to people, the rehabilitation of networks, the rehabilitation of the power station, the damage assessment of the buildings, the provision of portable clinics and schools. So there are concrete solutions, not rocket science, easy to implement. We just need the political will and the conditions for us to operate. And we can't wait for the big reconstruction to start immediately with early recovery because there are much more needs in Gaza beyond food, and I hope that we can establish the conditions in this area. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, where millions of people are internally displaced, UNOPS works with partners to provide income-generating infrastructure projects. This includes building schools, markets, youth centres and health clinics in the eastern part of the country, directly impacting 500,000— 650,000 people. Of course, this is also where much of the Ebola transmission is concentrated now, further complicating people's conditions and the delivery of our projects. In Afghanistan, as communities grapple with the impact of conflict, natural disasters and socio-economic challenges, my colleagues continue to manage the AWAZ Afghanistan, a call centre that serves as a crucial lifeline for Afghans, providing assistance, vital information and a platform to give feedback on humanitarian response and the delivery of basic services. With nearly 700,000 calls handled since it was launched in 2018, AWAS initiative has helped more than 5 million people across Afghanistan to access essential services and humanitarian aid. And you can see again, it's UNOPS supporting the people and enabling the other UN agencies, particularly humanitarian agencies, to operate. Across Latin America and the Caribbean, our efforts continue to strengthen health systems and improve equitable access to healthcare. In another example, UNOPS is supporting the Brazilian Cooperation Agency to deliver essential humanitarian assistance to countries affected by disasters and crises, from vaccines and medical supplies to food and water purifiers. UNOPS facilitated the procurement and delivery of critical supplies to 35 countries in emergency situations in 2025, including Caribbean nations affected by Hurricane Melissa. I had the chance in the first week after Hurricane Melissa severely affected Jamaica to be on the ground and to mobilize UNOPS team to conduct damage assessment. I used to mention this as an example of readiness. We are discussing this week and the last few weeks the reconfiguration of country teams. As you know, I've been leading that reform, and one of the elements that I always try to highlight is we shall not confuse residence with readiness. We shall be resident and present in many countries, and UN needs to find a way for many agencies to be resident and to be present. But in other cases, you don't need to be resident, you just need to be ready, and that's the case in Jamaica. We were not resident in Jamaica, but we were the agency that was called in the next— the first few hours about bringing the engineers that were fundamental to do damage assessment. So this is a good example of of not confusing residence with readiness. So that's why I'm so passionate, as you know, about the reconfiguration of country teams. I think it's a fundamental pillar of UN reform and we need to get it well. Mr. President, distinguished delegates, these are just a few examples of how UNOPS provides practical solutions across core areas of infrastructure procurement and project and fund management. UNOPS also hosts and supports a range of multilateral partnerships to advance global priorities. We host 14 entities, entities that are programmatic, we are non-programmatic, but we help them operate, which is a very important element of the network multilateralism. You don't need to be programmatic. We are non-programmatic and we don't want to be programmatic. We can't be programmatic.— that's not our mandate. But through our support on logistics, on financing, on administrative services, on procurement, we are enabling these hosted entities that are supported by Member States in delivering those programmes. Through these partnerships, we have helped improve global health, drive climate action, and accelerate sustainable development. This model allows critical partnerships to use our global presence and robust compliance frameworks to manage risk and deliver results transparently and effectively, creating faster and broader impact for communities around the world. Let me give you some examples, because this is not very often known. So who are the 14 OSAD entities? There are 14 OSCE entities that are supported by member states that we are very honored to host and to support them, in some cases in partnership with other agencies. For instance, the Santiago Network is supported by UNDRR and UNOPS. Let me now focus on a key element that you have been sharing with us, that is about collaboration in the UN, because this is one of the key mottos of the UN80, is to avoid fragmentation, to build coherence and collaboration across the system. As a key player within the UN system, UNOPS provides technical, operational, and logistical support that helps translate UN resolutions and mandates into tangible, on-the-ground results for communities we serve. How much do we deliver for the UN entities? 20%. So from our portfolio, 20% of everything we do is in support of UN entities. But more important is how much are we delivering with those entities, and that's 70%. So this is a very important element, is even if we are delivering indirect support to those UN agencies, 20% of our portfolio, in practical terms, even when we are not working for them, we are working with them.— and this is a key element of 70% of all our portfolio, when it's requested and supported by partner countries, by donor countries, by vertical funds, by IFIs— despite the origin of the demand is coming from non-UN, in practical terms 70% of everything we do, we do with UN, and I think that this is a good assessment and metric of collaboration. Honorable delegates, let me emphasize now the centrality of climate action to our work. UNOPS supports adaptation, mitigation, and loss and damage efforts. We help countries strengthen climate resilience, adapt, support the implementation of climate commitments, and we manage multi-stakeholder initiatives, including the Initiative for Climate Action Transparency. 2026 is a defining year for the climate agenda. As you know, I've been working on climate since '99, attended almost all COPs since '99 in multiple roles, and we knew that— the 1.5-degree objective by the end of the year would require tangible action and mutual accountability. Unfortunately, what the facts and the evidence is being shared with all of us is that we are overshooting. So the main conclusion of the last COP was— and it was a very important COP in Brazil, in Belém do Pará— is that we need to do more, that we are not on the path to 1.5, we are on the path to 2.3 to 2.5. So clearly the nationally determined contributions are not consistent with the agreement established in Paris a decade the goal. That's why 2026 is so important. It's the moment where we need to get it right. We need not only to revisit the National Determined Contributions and put them on the right path to 1.5, but it's also the moment where we need to implement the National Determined Contributions, and it's where UNEPS is ready to support Member States. Member States particularly developing countries, need support to accelerate the transition to renewable energy and invest in the infrastructure needed to make that transition work. That includes modernizing, expanding, and digitizing energy grids and scaling energy storage, as the grid infrastructure has simply not kept up with the remarkable growth in renewable generation. We have to do whatever we can on the supply side, but if we don't invest on grids and on storage, all efforts done on renewable energy and on supply will not make tangible results on climate mitigation and on the clean energy transition. Working with our partners, we have enhanced access to energy in rural communities in Sierra Leone, powered hospitals in Haiti, and improved access to essential services in Yemen. And we support efforts to create efficient and resilient grids around the world, including through our hosted partnerships such as Sustainable Energy for All and Southeast Asia Energy Transition Partnership. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, the impact I have described today is made possible by the trust of our partners. Results from the latest UNEPS Global Partner Survey shows strong trust in EUNOPS and growing demand for our integrated practical solutions. A record 85% of partners report satisfaction with EUNOPS. This is the best partner survey ever. A similar share say they would recommend the organization to others. Overall partners' trust in EUNOPS stands at 87%. This is the testament of commitment of UNOPS teams working in some of the world's most challenging and high-risk environments. They also speak to the progress achieved through our reforms, guided by you. There is no trust being rebuilt without a strong commitment on reform. Under the guidance of the Executive Board, we have over the past 3 years implemented a comprehensive programme of reforms that has delivered on our commitments, and seen these efforts recognized by third-party assessments. These measures have strengthened governance, accountability, and organizational performance, while enhancing ability to deliver results for communities and partners. And the results of the reforms are manifesting in other ways too—not only the partner survey, as I mentioned, But also our culture survey, our internal culture survey results, as my colleague Valérie Couchat has been sharing with you on other occasions, show encouraging progress. In 2025, participation reached a record 75%, with results showing progress in engagement, satisfaction, trust in local leadership, and transparency. The demand for EUNOP services is increasing, and this is another signal that we are getting the results of the reform. We saw it in the partner survey, we saw it in the culture survey, but also on the increasing demand. In 2025, we signed contracts at value of $3.4 billion, exceeding the implemented amount in that year. And just this year, I had with Carl, the CFO, and with the— the Sonja Leighton-Kohn a few days ago, we were checking the numbers for this year and we signed in the first semester of this year more contracts than in the comparable period in 2025 and in 2024. So clearly there is an increase. There is a growing demand from our partners, and those partners are from the UN and beyond the UN. Very often you ask me numbers about portfolio, so let me share some numbers. 20% of everything we do is for the UN. 14% is for programme countries, 15% for donor countries. So you can see that we get the demand and funding that is very relevant for partner countries. They use their own resources to ask the UNOPS to deliver, to implement their strategies. So 14% of everything is requested by the programme countries, 15% by donor countries, 18% vertical funds and multilateral initiatives, and 26% IFIs. International finance institutions, 6% regional and other international organizations. So you can see how relevant is our pipeline across the partnership. So the idea that we work only for the UN is not consistent. We work for the UN, we work with the UN,, but we basically support a multitude of partners that are, as you could see, revealing strong confidence on our work. That's why I would like to close precisely on this element of reforms. The results underscore the agility of the UNOPS demand-driven fee-for-service operating model. The model provides, as you know, full cost recovery and drives efficient resource management. It keeps the organization's overheads low and allows it to rapidly and efficiently respond to community needs and partners' demands. In an operational context where value for money is most critical, UNOPS continues to deliver projects with a full cost recovery fee of —on average, 4%. This is one of the lowest, if not the lowest, in the entire UN system. UROPS is an active supporter of the UN Haiti Reform Agenda and remains fully engaged across multiple work streams. At the request of the Secretary-General and under the leadership of the DSG, you know that I've coordinated the reconfiguration of country teams. And yesterday we had the chance with Mr. President to stress the relevance of connecting the conversation on the mergers with the conversations on reconfiguration of country teams, regional reset, thematic hubs, knowledge hubs, the funding compact, and expertise on demand. We will continue supporting this reform and we are confident that the reconfiguration of country teams will strengthen the resident coordinator and will maximize our capacity to deliver at scale, which is the reason why we exist. At these discussions— as these discussions continue, it is important to recognize the distinct added value of EUNOPS for Service demand-driven model and the contribution it makes to the efficient accountable implementation across the system. To conclude, Mr. President, distinguished members of the Executive Board, at a time of growing global crisis, shrinking financial resources, increasing threats to the United Nations, the collective responsibility is crystal clear. The UN is needed more than ever. Its demonstrable, practical solutions are needed more than ever. UNOPS will continue supporting people and partners across humanitarian, development and peacebuilding efforts, strengthening implementation capacity and efficient use of resources to bring tangible results to improve lives for communities. As we continue to advance the reform agenda and contribute to broader UN system reforms, I reiterate the support of UNOPS for a more effective, accountable an impactful United Nations. I would like to end by thanking you, Mr. President, and all member states for the strong support that you have been providing to UNEPS, and if you allow me, I would also like, in a session that is livestreamed, to thank the amazing work of my outstanding team working not only in headquarters but in more than 130 countries. Not the numbers of kilometres of roads, but also what is the impact of these roads that we are constructing on connecting people to the markets, connecting families to the schools, connecting economies to the ports to export goods and services. I really think that these two elements that I mentioned—reform and results—are the ingredients of trust. And it's not about UNOPS only. For someone that has been working on development for so many years, I consider that the more we do on delivering on the ground on results, and communicating and being accountable on those results. The more we do reforming the organizations and being accountable on that, the easier it will be to make the case for development cooperation and to ensure that taxpayers—because at the end of the day, it's what matters—taxpayers in partner countries with the Master Corps Service Mobilization and in donor countries with taxes from citizens are sufficiently confident that the results and the reforms are strong enough to continue retaining their support. That's why I always advise everyone to be very humble when we comment on ODA decline or any kind of discussions on development finance drop. We have to check and to ask ourselves what else can we do to ensure value for money? What else can we do to show through results and through reforms that each euro or dollar that is provided to a UN agency is leveraging local capacity, generating jobs, creating more local capacities to protect the planet and to deliver on the SDGs. So I really want to acknowledge the fact that so many delegations mentioned the topic of reforms and the topic of results. Mozambique on behalf of Africa made a very important point, if you allow me, on the cooperation frameworks, but also on energy. On the cooperation frameworks, and with the perspective of someone that has been working for one year on the reconfiguration of country teams in the UN system, The cooperation framework is the framework and should obviously be the framework to determine and to influence not only the relationship between the UN and the partner country, but also the relationship among the UN. So the cooperation framework shouldn't be just the relationship of UN country teams with the country, but also the way that the entire UN system, the agencies work together. And that's why I think that we have found a good compromise of retaining the country programme documents, because for many agencies that's not the case of UNOPS, because we don't have country programme documents, but there are a few agencies that have country programme documents and they consider those country programme documents as fundamental accountability tools to the boards and also important tools to mobilize resources. So I think that we have found a good compromise, which is showing that the Cooperation Framework is the strategic framework and the Country Programme Documents are ways to implement the Cooperation Framework through the specific mandates of each agency, which is assured making the Country Programme Documents being derived sequenced, and consulted. So country programme documents should derive from the cooperation framework. Country programme documents should be approved after the approval of the cooperation framework, and country programme documents shouldn't be a one-agency process, should be consulted with other agencies in the country, in the UN country team. So I really think that This is a fundamental pillar of the reform. I can't waste your time in going through this conversation, but I really believe that, as Mozambique was mentioning, that there is no possibility of reconfiguring country teams, making country teams really hubs for expertise on demand and regional reset, having modular approaches, avoiding a one-fit-all if at the end of the day we don't strengthen the resident coordinator and if we don't strengthen the cooperation framework. Second point that Mozambique mentioned is about energy, and indeed Africa is in a paradox context where it's home to 60% of solar potential and only attracts 1 to 3% of all investments on renewable energy. And that's why, again, we have to check what are we doing at UN to work together across the UN system and with international finance institutions to not only de-risk investment but to de-risk implementation in namely in Africa, not only on renewable energy but also on grids and storage. I speak in a very passionate manner about this topic because I don't think it is normal in the 21st century to have 700 million people without access to electricity and 2 billion people without access to clean cooking. So we may continue talking just about renewable energy, but it's fundamental to focus on grids and storage. For each dollar that is spent on renewable energy, only 60 cents is spent on grids and storage. So just investing on supply won't fix the issue. We just really need to work more on grids and on storage. And one of the reasons why I speak passionately about this topic is because the paradox of grids and storage is that it's state-owned. On the energy supply, you have more and more private sector investing with the right policy frameworks, with carbon pricing, with regulatory frameworks. You have more and more investment on renewable energy and it's the cheapest. But the problem is in most countries, in donor countries and in partner countries, in most countries grids are owned by the state because it's considered a natural monopoly and states want to preserve the grids to ensure that they preserve the sovereignty. So the fundamental problem here is how can we ask developing countries that are already highly indebted, that cannot pass to their consumers the investments made on grids because their consumers are already in a very vulnerable situation, how can we do it without concessional finance? And that's why the case for grids and storage is so important, and this connects a lot with my intervention yesterday when I said that one of the options in case we don't merge into a new agency, one of the options could be have a joint venture of UNOPS and UNDP on energy, on energy transition, because this could untap the potential for the supply of energy, the storage, the grids, and energy efficiency. So I want to thank Mozambique for bringing this topic of the energy poverty eradication nexus, the energy-climate nexus, and we can't overlook this. And again, we have to be humble. I insist on this point. How much investment is UNOPS and UNDP putting in place from the of the overall investment that is committed on clean energy, just 2%. And we are the largest, so in the UN system, UNOPS and UNDP are the agencies that do more on energy, but despite that, you can check, and only 2% of the entire commitment on energy is being done by these two agencies. At the same time, again, we have to be humble, and there are so many other agencies that play a fundamental role on energy: UNIDO, UNEP, UNFCCC, UNDESA, UNCTAD, and it's very important that— and I'm just mentioning a few— it's so important that we work together on this topic. There was a point that was made by Mozambique but also by several other delegations about how to ensure safeguards in case there is a merger. How can we safeguard not only the fee-for-service model, but also the specific interests of partner countries? And for me, this is the most important element. Regardless the modality of a merger, it's fundamental to ensure that when a country wants a school, it doesn't get an education policy. When a country wants an hospital, it doesn't get a health policy. And the country today may want a health policy and education policy and they go to UNDP. But what we must ensure that if a country has the education policy, the health policy, all policies, whole strategies, they don't need someone to partner with them on the design of a policy, they still have the chance. To choose the hospital and the school. And this is for me fundamental in the merger process. That's why the scenario of an acquisition, I think, it's a problem not for UNOPS, it's a problem for the countries because we would suddenly lose the neutrality, the independence, the demand-drivenness, the possibility to get the school or the hospital without getting the package., and that's why the merger into a new agency needs to preserve the balance between policy and delivery. So it's not delivery below policy, it's policy and delivery, it's integration and alignment. So this element of safeguards is not just safeguarding the fee-for-service and avoiding the projects of subsidized policy, it's also to ensure that from a conceptual point of view We continue serving you and we ensure that the organization will be able to continue responding to your specific requests. I think that I covered, when it comes to Bangladesh, the point on green technology, green transition, climate resilience. from my response to Mozambique, and we had the chance to meet yesterday and to take note of this graduation process to be deferred 3 years. You can continue counting on our support, and I always say that all world needs to learn about what is happening in Bangladesh on climate resilience and disaster risk resilience, because you have been affected by very difficult shocks on climate impacts, and there is lots of experience that we all can learn from disaster risk resilience. Brazil brought a very important point, if you allow me, which is why is Brazil asking us to put in place big infrastructure on an university? If there is a country in the world that has strong private sector on construction, on infrastructure, why UNOPS? Because Brazil basically wanted— and this is happening in many other countries— to have a neutral organisation to do project management. So rather than being the government interacting directly with the private sector, and to oversee the project implementation, you just decided to have a professional entity that knows about project management, you transfer to that entity the management of the project, and that entity takes the risk. So basically what we are doing, we take the risk. We take the risk and we take the responsibility. We charge a fee and we ensure that the timelines and the commitments, the financial commitments, are delivered. This is a very important element to make the case for project management, because we are getting this in many countries. How can we preserve localization of aid and at the same time having project management being deployed in the most efficient manner? And this connects with the question from the Russian Federation. Our strong commitment is with localization, and 50% of all procurement from UNOPS— 50% of all procurement from UNOPS is local. We buy locally, we procure locally, we recruit locally, and in some countries, for instance in Mozambique, in Cabo Delgado, it's more than 90%. So the localization of aid and localization of procurement is important, at the same time that we need a marketplace. And this allows me to connect directly with a point from the Russian Federation. If you allow me, I'm not going to elaborate on sustainable procurement because it's a conversation we have had in this room on many occasions, and there is of course some different views among member states on this specific point on sustainable procurement. We follow the norms, the guidelines from the UN and the SDG-rooted approaches, but there is one point that I would really like to make, which is how relevant is procurement for the SDGs. 15% to 20% of GDP in countries are connected with procurement. So procurement can be as important as 20% of an economy in a country. So the way we purchase, the way we buy, can have massive implications on gender equality, on sustainable development, on competitiveness, on transparency, on accountability. So the procurement element is not the technocratic, bureaucratic tool. It's really— can really make a difference on the SDGs. The UK— and again, I am not going to repeat my appreciation for many comments that were made from the delegations— you made a very important point about the efficiency agenda, because we tend— when we discuss reforms like UN 82, to start everything from a blank page. But in this case, we know what is needed. We just need to get it done. Common back offices, shared services, joint programming, pooled funding— those things are listed. There is a marketplace for that. It's fundamental that all agencies are accountable to you, Member States, on how much we do on support of these initiatives that are part of the BIG that is co-chaired by my colleague Sonja with her counterpart from UNFPA, Andrew. We can't live in an opt-out world. It's opt-in by default. I think— and apologies if I'm being outspoken, but I think it's better that I'm outspoken in an audience like this because we are accountable to you— I think that it's not normal, the number of common back offices that we have. It shouldn't be rocket science. Having the UN placed in the same place shared the premises and the services should be normal. But unfortunately, if you check the number of common back offices, it's still very small. So please, let's not just focus on UN80, on the new things. Let's make sure that the old things that are listed for many, many years get the traction and get implemented. And I think that we are accountable, of course, to you in these aspects. I think that I covered the important points made by Germany on results, but you made an important point about accountability, and I want to stress that all projects from UNOPS are linked to SDGs. We measure and assess all projects on the basis of our mandate and SDGs. But also that 97% of the internal oversight measures are implemented. So only one is open. So in the last 18 months, 97% of the internal oversight recommendations are implemented. So this, I hope, can show how committed we continue on accountability and even 2 weeks ago at the management team, we discussed a new framework for accountability to ensure that based on the Strategic Plan 26-29, and the Chief of Staff Ilary Balbuena is overseeing this process, based on the Strategic Plan 26-29, we have a battery of indicators of accountability to report on our project. So we consider accountability is not just a reporting tool to you on the project, is also a way to ensure that each member of the UNEPS team is accountable on its contribution to the specific deliverables of the Strategic Plan 2026-2029. Apologies, Mr. President, I will try to be quick. Nepal made an important reference to sustainable infrastructure. And again, how much— how relevant is sustainable infrastructure? Infrastructure represents 92% of all SDGs and roughly 80% of greenhouse gas emissions. So the case for infrastructure is fundamental on climate and on sustainability. But other element that I think is somehow overlooked is the infrastructure as a nexus or as a glue, as an integrator. We live in discussions that very often are fragmented. We go to a place and we talk humanitarian. We go to another place and we talk development, peace and security. We go to a place and we talk loss and damage, mitigation, adaptation. We go to a place and we talk policy, finance, and delivery. Infrastructure is really an integrator. If we get it right, we can have sustainable and resilient infrastructure which is key for mitigation, adaptation, and loss and damage. If we get it right, we have infrastructure that is good to address humanitarian needs, early recovery, and development. If we get it right, we have infrastructure that is designed in ways that are bankable and are implementable, so you have the policy, the finance, and implementation integrated. So I really think that, Mr. President, if there is a topic that I would I think would be important to any kind of interactive dialogue in this Board— and apologies if I'm stepping out of my role because it's up to the Board— it's infrastructure. Infrastructure is an element of multiple collaboration in the UN system and I think that it's an area where all agencies will have something relevant to say. The United States made a fundamental point on value for money. I never like UNEPS to be presented as a cheap organization because that's not the value of UNEPS, but indeed the fact that we charge on average 4% speaks to the frugality of the way we deliver. For instance, how can we just charge 4% on average. Of course, this is connected with our business model, with our layout of operations, but also making good judgment of the presence on the ground. We don't get directors in all countries. We have the resident coordinator. If we have the resident coordinator in a country,— that's the resident coordinator that can help us making the political conversations with the government. So I prefer to have engineers. Of course, in some countries we have directors, we have multi-country offices with directors, but in most countries we don't have directors, we don't have D2s or D1s. UNOPS, out of the 6,000 personnel, we have 50 D1s and above. This shows how frugal and how good judgment I think we make of the resources we use. How do we do it? Of course, we have more multi-country offices, we have the critical mass at the multi-country offices, we use the multi-country offices to deploy the surge that is needed to the countries, and then we rely on resident coordinators. That's why I've been saying for more than a year that in my opinion, but it's just my opinion, the Resident Coordinator should be the most senior person in a country, should be the ambassador of the entire UN to the country, and we should work for the Resident Coordinator and the Resident Coordinator should work for us. And it's the way I see the Resident Coordinator. I see the Resident Coordinator as being part of my team, and I also see my team being part of the team of the Resident Coordinator. So talking about fees and frugality and value for money, and of course I'm using the question from the US to make a reference to the Resident Coordinator, I think it's really important that we empower the Resident Coordinators as the integrator, as the honest broker, as the real coordinator, the person that tells an agency, 'Please stop, this is not your mandate. Please stop, you have to stop competing and let's find ways to work together. So I think that part of the solution for value for money is ensuring that we make even more use of the Resident Coordinator. I think that I responded to the important question from the EU on infrastructure and Global Gateway when I responded to Nepal. I think that this element was made. The European Union mentioned that EUNOPS is present in all pillars, and indeed I'm not doing a PR operation here, but if you check the report from the Secretary-General on UN80, the first report with facts and figures, you have several UN agencies that work on humanitarian and development, you have several UN agencies that work on humanitarian and peace and security, but you have only one organization that works simultaneously on peace and security, humanitarian, and development, and that's UNOPS. And I think that this is a key element when it comes to conversations on UN80, is this role of UNOPS cutting across the pillars and enabling others to operate. Thank you, Mr. Vice President, distinguished members of the Executive Board, colleagues. Good morning, good afternoon, wherever you're watching from. I'm pleased to present an update on the UNOPS Global Mobility Framework, developed in response to Executive Board Decision 2025/19. At its core, this framework is about ensuring that UNOPS has the agile, globally connected, and future-ready workforce required to deliver effectively for our partners and the communities we serve. In developing the framework, we undertook a comprehensive review of our workforce data and organizational trends. Our objective was to design an approach that is evidence-based, practical, and aligned with the unique business model of UNOPS. The analysis confirmed that UNOPS is already a relatively mobile organization. Most international personnel move regularly through their careers, at the average tenure in a position of 2.8 years. At the same time, the data highlighted areas where increased mobility would strengthen organizational effectiveness. Approximately 10% of our international personnel have remained in the same position for 7 years or more, primarily at senior levels and in headquarter locations. We also found that nearly half of our global leadership network has served in only one duty station during their UNOPS career. These patterns matter because mobility is not simply about movement. It is about strengthening leadership, building skills, broadening perspectives, facilitating knowledge transfer, and creating opportunities for talent development across the organization. It is also about building stronger connections between headquarters and the field. The framework therefore establishes a flexible vacancy-based approach that balances organizational needs with individual career aspirations. International personnel will generally be expected to move within a 3 to 6 year period with a maximum tenure of 7 years in any one position. The approach is phased and supported by talent management measures designed to encourage and facilitate mobility over time. Since presenting the framework to the Board in February, we have made significant progress. Our Talent Plus recruitment system and onboarding platform is now operational and provides an important foundation for implementation. Development of a talent marketplace which will serve as the mobility framework's digital engine is also progressing well and remains on track for launch later this year. Mobility considerations are being integrated into talent acquisition and performance management policies and into workforce planning and budgeting processes. This is an important step in ensuring that mobility becomes part of how we strategically manage our workforce. We have also begun implementing leadership mobility through a number of voluntary rotations and post swaps, with additional senior leadership rotations planned during 2026 and early 2027. These early movements demonstrate our commitment to leading by example. Engagement with personnel remains a priority., and consultations will continue throughout the transition period. Implementation will be phased over 2026 and 2027, as I mentioned, and monitored through a set of key performance indicators. By 2027, we aim to reduce the proportion of personnel serving more than 7 years in the same position from 10% to 7%, with a longer-term target of 2% by 2030. Sorry. Mr. President and distinguished members of the Executive Board, our Executive Director has consistently underscored building a mobile workforce is not simply a talent management objective. It is a strategic investment in leadership, organizational effectiveness, and the long-term sustainability of UNOPS. Mobility enables us to bring diverse perspectives together, strengthen connections between headquarters and the field, and ensure that our leaders are equipped to respond to increasingly complex operational challenges. This framework represents an important investment in the future of UNOPS. It will help us build a workforce that is adaptable, connected, and equipped to meet the increasingly complex challenges of the environments in which we operate. We remain— in closing, Mr. Chairman— we remain committed to implementing the framework in a transparent, fair, and accountable manner, and we welcome the continued engagement and guidance of the Executive Board. Thank you, Mr. President.
